ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteology:
Why this matters: the anterior abdominal wall is a layered muscular sheet whose aponeuroses build the rectus sheath and the inguinal canal — the weak points where hernias appear. Master the nine regions, the wall layers, the rectus sheath (arcuate line) and the inguinal canal/hernias, and surface anatomy, incisions and groin lumps all make sense.
Regions & Surface Anatomy
The nine regions
  • Two vertical (midclavicular) and two horizontal planes divide the abdomen into 9 regions
  • Top: right hypochondrium · epigastrium · left hypochondrium
  • Middle: right lumbar (flank) · umbilical · left lumbar
  • Bottom: right iliac (inguinal) · hypogastrium (suprapubic) · left iliac
Key planes & landmarks
  • Transpyloric plane of Addison (L1) — midway xiphisternum→umbilicus; pylorus, fundus of gallbladder, pancreatic neck, SMA origin, hila of kidneys
  • Subcostal (L3) & transtubercular (L5) planes; the McBurney’s point (⅓ from ASIS to umbilicus) overlies the appendix base
Layers of the Anterior Abdominal Wall
Superficial → deep
  • Skin
  • Superficial fascia: Camper’s (fatty, superficial) & Scarpa’s (membranous, deep) — below the umbilicus
  • Muscles (with their investing fasciae)
  • Transversalis fascia → extraperitoneal fat → parietal peritoneum
Scarpa’s continuity
  • Scarpa’s fascia continues into the perineum as Colles’ fascia and onto the penis/scrotum (dartos)
  • Explains how extravasated urine (ruptured spongy urethra) tracks into the scrotum & up the abdominal wall
The Muscles
MuscleFibre directionNote
External obliqueInferomedial (“hands in pockets”)Aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament
Internal obliqueSuperomedial (at right angles to EO)Contributes to the conjoint tendon
Transversus abdominisTransverse (horizontal)Deepest; contributes to the conjoint tendon
Rectus abdominisVertical (paired straps)Tendinous intersections; flexes the trunk
The three flat muscles' aponeuroses enclose rectus abdominis as the rectus sheath and fuse in the midline as the linea alba; the lateral edge of rectus abdominis is the linea semilunaris. All are innervated by the anterior rami of T7–T12 (& L1).
The Rectus Sheath & Arcuate Line
Above the arcuate line
  • The internal oblique aponeurosis splits around rectus abdominis
  • Anterior wall: external oblique + anterior lamina of internal oblique
  • Posterior wall: posterior lamina of internal oblique + transversus abdominis
Below the arcuate line
  • All three aponeuroses pass anterior to rectus abdominis
  • The posterior wall is just transversalis fascia (a potential weak point)
  • The arcuate line lies ~⅓ of the way from umbilicus to pubis
The Inguinal Canal
Rings & walls
  • An oblique ~4 cm passage above the inguinal ligament; the deep ring (in transversalis fascia, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels) → the superficial ring (a defect in the EO aponeurosis)
  • Anterior wall: EO aponeurosis (+ IO laterally)
  • Posterior wall: transversalis fascia (+ conjoint tendon medially)
  • Roof: arching fibres of IO & TA · Floor: inguinal ligament (+ lacunar ligament medially)
Contents
  • The spermatic cord (♂) or the round ligament of the uterus (♀)
  • The ilioinguinal nerve (enters through the superficial ring; lies on the cord, not within it)
The inguinal ligament is the rolled-under lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis, running from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the pubic tubercle.
The Spermatic Cord
Contents (rule of 3s)
  • 3 arteries: testicular, cremasteric, artery to the vas deferens
  • 3 nerves: genital branch of the genitofemoral (the nerve to cremaster), sympathetic fibres, & the ilioinguinal nerve (which runs on the cord, not within its coverings)
  • 3 other: vas (ductus) deferens, pampiniform plexus of veins, lymphatics
3 coverings (from 3 layers)
  • External spermatic fascia — from external oblique
  • Cremasteric fascia — from internal oblique (& the cremaster muscle)
  • Internal spermatic fascia — from transversalis fascia
Inguinal Hernias & Hesselbach’s Triangle
Hesselbach’s (inguinal) triangle
  • Medial: lateral border of rectus abdominis
  • Lateral: inferior epigastric vessels
  • Inferior: inguinal ligament
  • A direct hernia pushes through this triangle
Indirect vs direct
  • Indirect (commonest) — through the deep ring, LATERAL to the inferior epigastric vessels; congenital (patent processus vaginalis); can enter the scrotum
  • Direct — through Hesselbach’s triangle, MEDIAL to the inferior epigastric vessels; acquired (weak wall)
Reduce & occlude the deep ring. If pressure over the deep ring (just above the mid-inguinal point / the femoral pulse) controls a reduced hernia, it is indirect; a direct hernia still bulges. A hernia below & lateral to the pubic tubercle is femoral; above & medial is inguinal.
The Posterior Abdominal Wall
Psoas major — from the lumbar vertebrae to the lesser trochanter (with iliacus = iliopsoas, the chief hip flexor); a psoas abscess tracks to the groin.
Quadratus lumborum — 12th rib & lumbar transverse processes to the iliac crest; laterally flexes the trunk.
Iliacus — the iliac fossa to the lesser trochanter.
The umbilical folds on the inner wall: median (urachus), medial (obliterated umbilical arteries) & lateral (inferior epigastric vessels).
Clinical Correlations
Incisions — midline (through linea alba, avascular), gridiron/McBurney (appendix), Pfannenstiel (suprapubic, obstetric/pelvic), paramedian.
Rectus sheath haematoma — torn inferior epigastric vessels below the arcuate line → a painful mass mimicking an acute abdomen.
Caput medusae — dilated para-umbilical veins in portal hypertension (portosystemic anastomosis).
Divarication of recti — stretched linea alba (pregnancy) → a midline bulge on sitting up.
Referred pain — the umbilicus is the T10 dermatome (early appendicitis pain).
🧠 Mnemonics
Spermatic cord coverings — “Externally, Cremaster Internally”: External spermatic (EO), Cremasteric (IO), Internal spermatic (transversalis).
Indirect = lateral to the inferior epigastric; direct = medial (MDs don’t lie: Medial = Direct).
Rectus sheath below the arcuate line — all aponeuroses go in front.
Cord contents — 3 arteries, 3 nerves, 3 others (rule of threes).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Nine regions divided by 2 midclavicular & 2 horizontal planes; transpyloric plane = L1.
Superficial fascia below umbilicus = Camper’s (fatty) + Scarpa’s (membranous).
External oblique fibres point inferomedially (“hands in pockets”).
Below the arcuate line, all three aponeuroses lie anterior to rectus; posterior wall = transversalis fascia.
Deep ring = lateral to inferior epigastric; superficial ring = defect in EO aponeurosis.
Inguinal ligament = EO aponeurosis, ASIS → pubic tubercle.
Indirect hernia = lateral to inferior epigastric (through deep ring, congenital); direct = medial (Hesselbach’s, acquired).
Hernia below & lateral to the pubic tubercle = femoral; above & medial = inguinal.
Ilioinguinal nerve lies on the cord, not within it.
Abdominal wall innervation = T7–T12 & L1 anterior rami.
